fix: fill a vector path from its exact coverage, not aggdraw's dilation

aggdraw offsets a filled path outward by a quarter pixel with a miter
contour before rasterizing it, so it reports a quarter pixel of coverage
on every side that is not there. Measured, not inferred: sweeping a
straight edge shows coverage = area + 0.25 clamped; a sliver of area 0.1
lands as 0.6, which a constant added to coverage cannot do; the convex
corner of a pixel-aligned square reads 15/255 against 15.9 predicted by
a miter offset and 12.5 by a round one; the concave corner of an L reads
111 against 111.5. A Pen is exact -- width 1 covers exactly 1 -- so it
is only the brush, and there is no Python-visible way to turn it off.

Fill instead by signed-area accumulation: cut every segment at the pixel
boundaries it crosses, credit each piece dy * (1 - x) to its own cell
and dy to everything right of it, and prefix-sum along the row. That is
the area, exactly, and it does not depend on where on the grid the path
sits. Pieces are cut and summed a band of rows at a time, which bounds
peak memory independently of the canvas: a 5000-segment path across
3300x5100 peaks at 194 MB where the unbanded form took 5.3 GB.

A combined path is now filled as one path under the non-zero rule
rather than a subpath at a time unioned, so a subpath wound against its
neighbour cuts a hole instead of being swallowed.

Against Photoshop's own raster of each unstroked vector-masked layer in
the corpus, 415 of 458 now land within 1/255 where 20 did; the median
error goes 0.0144 to 0.0000074. effects/stroke-effect-transparent-shape
returns to 1.268e-11 under force=True, the regression #844 reports.

aggdraw still draws the pen, so a stroke still needs it; filling a path
no longer does.

fix: fill a combined path even-odd, which is what Photoshop does

The previous commit filled a combined path by the non-zero rule and said
Photoshop does. It does not, and the claim had no oracle behind it: the
corpus cannot tell the two rules apart, because Photoshop cuts a hole by
reversing the subpath that makes it, and where the windings oppose each
other even-odd and non-zero agree. psd_tools.api.shape.VectorMask.paths
has said "In PSD, path fill rule is even-odd" the whole time, and the
format specification says the same.

So Photoshop was asked. Two nested rectangles were forged into one
component of transparentbg.psd's layer, once wound alike and once
against, and Photoshop 2026 rasterized both. It returned the same ring
either way -- 3000 pixels, the 4200 of the outer rectangle less the 1200
of the inner -- where non-zero would have filled the same-wound one

fix: rebuild the donor's record list on a cross-document move

`GroupMixin.extend()` and `insert()` called `self._psd._update_record()`
only, so moving a layer into another document rebuilt the receiving
document's flat record list and left the donor's holding the layer.
`PSDImage.save()` writes that stored list without rebuilding it on any
path, so saving the donor afterwards wrote the layer back into it and
the layer ended up in both files. `remove()`, `pop()` and `clear()` were
already correct, because the donor is `self` there.

Both methods now also rebuild each distinct donor document whose `_psd`
is not the receiving one, which `append()` inherits through `extend()`.
That rebuild calls `mark_updated()` too, so the donor's `save()`
regenerates a preview that no longer shows the layer.

The donor's document is read inside the detach loop rather than off the
`donors` list afterwards: `_update_children()` repoints a moved layer's
`_psd` at the receiving document, and a donor group that is itself one
of the moved layers would by then name the wrong one. A same-document
move captures nothing, so it still rebuilds once.

The in-memory tree was already right, so the test saves and reopens the
*donor*. It moves through all three entry points separately -- reverting
either half of the fix alone fails it -- and uses a shipped fixture as
the donor so that the dirty flag starts clear.

Merge pull request #865 from psd-tools/fix/authoritative-layer-info-861

fix: rebuild the layer list the reader actually consults

fix: write the regenerated preview at the document's own depth

`PSDImage.save()` rebuilt the merged image data section by rendering the
composite to a PIL image and splitting that. A PIL image describes PIL, not
the document, and every way the two differ became a defect in the file:

- one byte per channel whatever the header's depth says, so a 16-bit
  document's section came out half its declared length and a 32-bit one a
  quarter. psd-tools cannot read its own output back, and Photoshop rejects
  the file outright where there are no layers to rebuild the composite from
- only the channels PIL's mode has a letter for, so a document with spot
  channels or a second alpha wrote four planes of six or seven and the RLE
  decoder filled the rest with black
- `Image.tobytes()` on mode "1" leaves the bit clear for black where the
  format sets it, so every bitmap document was stored as its own negative
- `convert("P")` quantizes onto PIL's web palette rather than the document's
  colour table, so an indexed document came back in unrelated colours
- `pil_io.post_process()` inverts a CMYK image, and the render applies the
  ICC profile the document still carries, so a profiled CMYK preview was
  stored as the ink complement of an sRGB conversion
- PIL's RGBA is unpremultiplied where the stored preview is composited over
  white, leaving the reader to divide out an alpha the values had never been
  multiplied by

Measured over the 302-file fixture corpus: 33 files wrote a section that did
not match their own header, and none do now. Of the files whose preview can
be read both before and after, 95 round-trip closer and none further.

The planes are built from the compositor's arrays instead, through
`numpy_io.encode_image_data()` -- the inverse of `get_image_data()`, plane by
plane through `_encode_array()`, the inverse of `_parse_array()`. Channels the
compositor cannot produce are carried over from the stored preview rather than
regenerated, and are dropped rather than carried when it fails to decode.

`ImageData.new()` is fixed in the same pass: it packed a depth-32 fill as the
integer 0xffffffff, which is a quiet NaN read back as a float, so a document
`PSDImage.new(depth=32)` built was NaN before it was ever saved.

Fixes #866

fix: write the regenerated preview at the document's own depth

fix: write layer channels at the document's depth, not PIL's

Every API path that builds channel data from a PIL image took the depth
from the image. A PIL image holds a byte per pixel whatever it describes,
so a 16- or 32-bit document was given channels a half or a quarter of the
length its geometry requires, and the layer read back empty. This is the
rule #866 fixed for the merged image data section, in the layer path.

Three places share it:

- `_build_layer_record_and_channels()` took `get_pil_depth()`, which
  reports 8 for every mode `frompil()` can produce. It now takes the
  destination header's depth, and packs through `pil_io.encode_channel()`
  -- `numpy_io._encode_array()`, the exact inverse of the reader's
  `_parse_array()`, so 128 is stored as 32896 at depth 16.

- `_make_mask_channel_data()` hardcoded 8, on a docstring claim that a
  mask is always 8-bit. It is not: 24 masks in the corpus are 16-bit and
  two are 32-bit, and `get_layer_data()` reads a mask channel at
  `layer._psd.depth` like any other.

- `_convert_mode()` guarded on `pil_mode` alone, so a layer moved between
  two RGB documents of different depths was carried across in the source's
  packing; and it re-encoded with the *source* document's version, so a
  PSD-to-PSB move left two-byte RLE row counts in a four-byte file. Both
  read back black. Depth- and version-only moves now repack each channel
  in place, which leaves the layer record alone -- the `pil_mode` branch
  rebuilds it, and so drops the layer's opacity, blend mode and mask, and
  it fires on exactly the moves it fired on before.

Depth 1 is repaired incidentally: the opaque transparency channel was
`b"\xff"` per pixel, four times too long and, read as bits, fully
transparent. A "1" band is normalised to "L" before packing, since its
`tobytes()` is bit-packed and only accidentally a byte per pixel; and ZIP
with prediction, which has no depth-1 branch, is downgraded to plain ZIP
rather than raising out of `set_data()`.

Also fixes a `ValueError` on a "P" image carrying an `info["transparency"]`
key: `has_transparency_data` is true of one, and there is no "A" band to
index.

ci: do not read a failed milestone lookup as a missing milestone

The step's default shell is bash -e with no pipefail, so in

    NUM=$(gh api ... | head -n 1)

the pipeline's status is head's. A gh call that fails without stdout left
NUM empty and the step announced "nothing to close" -- the silent no-close
the warning added in the previous commit exists to prevent.

parameter expansion rather than head: under --paginate, head exiting early
would SIGPIPE gh, which an explicit status check would then misread as a
failure. The multi-match guard is unchanged in effect.

failure warns and exits 1, an absent milestone is a clean no-op, two
milestones sharing a title resolve to one PATCH, a failed PATCH warns, and
the happy path closes. continue-on-error still keeps a tagged release green.

fix: composite a layer's effects into the layer, not onto the backdrop

Compositor._apply_effects() ran after the layer was already in the
backdrop, so a stroke or overlay blended against the finished composite
rather than against the layer it belongs to. Where the layer's coverage
is partial that leaves a backdrop term in every pixel of the effect:
an outset stroke came out at t*S + (1 - t)*(alpha*L + (1 - alpha)*B)
where Photoshop renders alpha*L + (1 - alpha)*S.

Effects now composite into the layer's own source, which _EffectCanvas
holds, and the layer and its effects reach the canvas as one source.
An effect lands in one of two places relative to the layer's region:

- over(), inside it: an overlay, or the part of a stroke within the
  boundary. It paints over the layer and knocks out what it covers.
- beside(), outside it: the part of a stroke past the boundary. Its
  coverage adds to the layer's rather than being unioned with it,
  because a band drawn from the layer's own coverage is complementary
  to it -- on a pixel the boundary cuts, an outset band comes out at
  1 - alpha and the two together fill the pixel.

draw_stroke_effect_split() divides the band at the boundary as a share
of what draw_stroke_effect() draws, so the halves always sum to it, and
the part of an inner band that falls where the layer has no paint --
reachable when a stroke traces the mask rather than the layer -- paints
beside the layer rather than being dropped.

Fill opacity fades the layer's paint and not its effects, which the old
order got for free; the canvas folds it into the layer's own paint and
carries the coverage a knockout punches with in _Source.knockout_shape.

Measured over the fixture corpus in both force modes, 9 documents move
nearer Photoshop's preview and 3 further. feathered-stroke.psd goes
1.6e-3 -> 9.9e-5, antialiased-stroke-edge.psd 6.0e-4 -> 1.0e-4, and
shape-fx2.psd 6.6e-4 -> 8.8e-5 with its alpha at 9.1e-8. Per layer, the
four soft-edged pixel layers of stroke-effects.psd go 4.8e-3..4.0e-2 to
1.3e-5 and better, one of them bit for bit. The three that move further
are each a pre-existing coverage error the correct order stops
cancelling: clipping-mask2.psd applies a shape layer's vector mask twice,
shape-fx2.psd under force=True rasterizes its polygon 0.33 where
Photoshop has 0.70, and layer_params.psb is text psd-tools cannot set.

Merging the outer half of a stroke into the layer's source handed it the

and the knockout punches with the layer's own coverage again. A

fix(security): guard thumbnail() against unvalidated header dimensions

ThumbnailResource.read() takes width/height straight from the thumbnail
image-resource header without comparing them to the resource's actual
payload length. convert_thumbnail_to_pil() then fed those dimensions

get_pil_channels() undercounts several PIL modes it was never meant to
classify this way: it has no RGBA entry (falls back to 3, actual 4 bytes/px)
and counts "I"/"F" as 1 channel despite their 32-bit depth (actual 4

format, and mode, from thumbnail.data's own header -- an attacker can pick
any format Pillow supports and undercount the true allocation by up to 4x,
bypassing max_alloc_bytes.

image in the same mode reports the exact bytes-per-pixel Pillow will
allocate, whatever the mode. Add regression tests pinning both undercounted

Image.open() with no format hint tries every registered Pillow plugin
against thumbnail.data. Some plugins decode pixels inside their own

image's header could ever run, so the guard added for the fmt=1 branch
did not cover every format Pillow can be tricked into trying.

to Image.open() so no other plugin ever runs against the payload. Replace

pinning the ICO payload's rejection.

fix(security): count Pillow's real 4-byte-per-pixel storage, not tobytes()

len(Image.new(mode, (1,1)).tobytes()) measures the *serialized* width, not
what Pillow allocates internally. Verified by RSS measurement across every
mode JPEG can decode to (isolated subprocess per mode, avoiding
high-water-mark noise across allocations): "1"/"L"/"P" store one byte per
pixel; RGB, RGBA, CMYK, LA, I and F all measure ~4 bytes/pixel internally,
padding included, even where tobytes() serializes fewer (RGB: 3, LA: 2).

That meant the RGB estimate -- the common case -- undercounted the real
allocation by 25%. Replace the tobytes() probe with the measured rule
directly, and add a regression pinning RGB's real 4-byte-per-pixel budget
rather than its serialized 3.

feat: default the allocation budget to 4 GiB and make it settable

environment variable. It now defaults to 4 GiB, "unlimited" disables it in
the API and the environment, and PSDImage.max_alloc_bytes changes it after
opening. None keeps deferring to MAX_ALLOC_BYTES at check time. Invalid API
values raise before the file is read; an invalid environment or module value
warns and falls back to the default, so the composite path's ValueError and
TypeError handlers cannot swallow it.

what it does not.
